items.title: Focus Question: What are some common kinds of waves?

answer.html: Transverse waves (a shaken rope, light), longitudinal waves (sound in air, a pushed coiled spring toy), and surface waves on water. All of them carry energy from place to place without carrying the medium along.

items.title: Figure 6 caption: Classify each wave as transverse or longitudinal and explain: (i) a sound wave from a speaker, (ii) a wave sent along a rope by flicking one end sideways, (iii) a stretch-and-release pulse sent down a coiled spring toy.

answer.html: (i) Longitudinal: air molecules vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the sound travels, making compressions and rarefactions. (ii) Transverse: the rope moves sideways, perpendicular to the direction the pulse travels. (iii) Longitudinal: the coils move parallel to the spring's length, bunching up (compressions) and spreading out (stretches).

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2): A student plucks a guitar string harder so the vibration is larger, then plucks again after tuning the string to a higher frequency (without changing its tension). What happens to the wave speed in the string in each case?

answer.html: Plucking harder only increases the amplitude, and the speed is unchanged. Changing the frequency alone does not change the speed either, because the speed is set by the string's tension and mass per length; the wavelength changes to keep 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 the same. (If the tuning is done by raising tension, the speed does change, but that is changing the medium.)

items.title: Figure 10 caption: Determine the period, frequency, wavelength and speed of a rope wave described by these graphs: the displacement-versus-time graph at one point on the rope has crests at 𝑡= 0.30 s and 𝑡= 0.90 s; the displacement-versus-position graph at one instant has crests at 𝑥= 0.40 m and 𝑥= 1.30 m.

body.html: Time between successive crests = 0.90 s −0.30 s. Distance between successive crests = 1.30 m −0.40 m.
Period is the time for one cycle, wavelength is the distance for one cycle, 𝑓= 1 / 𝑇, and 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆.

check.html: 𝜆/ 𝑇= 0.90 / 0.60 = 1.5 m/s, the same speed.

items.title: 14: A church bell is heard 612 m away 1.80 s after it rings. Its frequency is 262 Hz. Find (a) the speed of the sound, (b) its period, (c) its wavelength.

body.html: 𝛥𝑑= 612 m, 𝛥𝑡= 1.80 s, 𝑓= 262 Hz. Find 𝑣, 𝑇, 𝜆.
𝑣= 𝛥𝑑/ 𝛥𝑡, 𝑇= 1 / 𝑓, 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓.

answer.html: 𝑇= 3.82 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> s

check.html: 340 m/s is close to the speed of sound in air at room temperature, and 𝑓𝜆= 262 × 1.30 = 341 m/s.

items.title: 15: A wave on a rope passes into a thinner, lighter rope tied to it. Which of 𝑣, 𝑓, 𝜆 change, and why?

answer.html: The wave source sets the frequency, so 𝑓 stays the same. The speed depends on the medium, so 𝑣 changes (a wave on a lighter rope moves faster). Since 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 with 𝑓 fixed, 𝜆 changes in the same direction as 𝑣 (here, longer in the lighter rope).

items.title: 16: A water wave has frequency 2.80 Hz and wavelength 0.450 m. What is its speed? 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆= (2.80 Hz)(0.450 m) = 1.26 m/s
17: A wave on a rope has its wavelength decreased by 25 percent while the rope stays the same. What happens to the frequency?

body.html: The rope sets the speed, so it stays constant; 𝑓= 𝑣/ 𝜆.

answer.html: The frequency increases by a factor of 4 / 3 (about a 33% increase).

items.title: 18: A wave travels at 24.0 m/s along a cable with a frequency of 8.00 Hz. What is its wavelength?
19: A wave generator in a ripple tank makes seven wavelengths every 0.250 s. The wavelength is 2.40 cm. How fast do the waves travel?

body.html: Frequency 𝑓= 7 / 0.250 s = 28.0 Hz. Then:

check.html: Equivalent: seven wavelengths = 16.8 cm in 0.250 s = 0.672 m/s.

items.title: 20: A longitudinal wave on a coiled spring toy has a frequency of 12.0 Hz, and successive compressions are 0.350 m apart. What is its speed?

body.html: The distance between successive compressions is one wavelength.

items.title: 21: What happens to the frequency of a wave when its period triples?

answer.html: The frequency becomes one-third as large.

items.title: 22: What happens to the wavelength of a wave in a given medium when its period is reduced to one-third of its original value?

body.html: 𝜆= 𝑣𝑇 and 𝑣 is fixed by the medium.

answer.html: The wavelength is cut to one-third.

items.title: 23: A wave's speed drops to 0.60 times its original value while its frequency stays the same. What happens to the wavelength?

answer.html: The wavelength decreases to 0.60 of its original value (40% shorter).

items.title: 24 (Challenge): A hiker shouts toward a canyon wall 380 m away and hears the echo 2.30 s later. The sound has a wavelength of 0.620 m. Find (a) the speed of sound, (b) its frequency, (c) its period.

body.html: The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is 2(380 m) = 760 m. 𝛥𝑡= 2.30 s, 𝜆= 0.620 m.

answer.html: 𝑓= 533 Hz
𝑇= 1.88 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> s

check.html: 330 m/s is close to the speed of sound in cool air (about 0 °C).

items.title: 25: Demonstrate that a longitudinal wave transports energy but not matter.

answer.html: Tie a bright ribbon to one coil in the middle of a long coiled spring toy lying on a smooth floor. Push and pull the end along the spring's length to send a pulse. The pulse travels the whole spring, but the ribbon only moves back and forth along the spring and ends up where it started (no matter moved along). Energy transport: the pulse reaching the far end knocks over a light block placed against it, or your partner feels a push on their hand.

items.title: 26: A student shakes a rope more slowly (half the frequency) with the same hand motion. How do the amplitude, frequency, period, speed and wavelength change?

body.html: Amplitude is set by the hand's distance, frequency by the hand (source), speed by the rope, and 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓.

answer.html: Amplitude: unchanged. Frequency: halves. Period: doubles. Speed: unchanged (rope's property). Wavelength: doubles, since 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓 with 𝑣 fixed.

items.title: 27: Describe transverse waves. Which kinds of media can carry them?

answer.html: In a transverse wave the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, as in a shaken rope or a wave along a guitar string. Transverse waves travel through solids (which resist shearing), and along the surface of a liquid. They do not travel through the interior of a gas or liquid, because those cannot supply a sideways restoring force.

items.title: 28: A pulse is sent along a steel guitar string, a loose clothesline, and a coiled spring toy, all about 3 m long. Rank the pulse speeds and explain.

answer.html: Fastest to slowest: steel guitar string (tight, stiff, and light, so its speed is high), then the clothesline, then the coiled spring toy (slow enough to watch the pulse travel). Wave speed on a string rises with the tension and falls with the mass per length, so tight, thin strings carry pulses quickly and loose, heavy ones slowly.

items.title: 29 (Critical Thinking): Hundreds of small boats bobbing around a harbor do not produce large waves, yet one large ferry arriving makes a big wake. Why?

answer.html: Each small boat transfers little energy, so each makes only a tiny wave. They bob at random places and times, so their waves are out of phase and partly cancel (destructive interference) instead of adding up. The ferry delivers a lot of energy in one coordinated disturbance, so the wave amplitude is large. Waves grow when the driving is coordinated (in phase), not random.

items.title: Focus Question: What are some common types of waves?

answer.html: Transverse waves (rope, light), longitudinal waves (sound, a coiled spring toy), and surface waves (water), all of which carry energy without carrying matter.

items.title: Figure 6 caption: Explain the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves.

answer.html: In a transverse wave the medium is disturbed perpendicular to the direction the wave travels (rope shaken up and down). In a longitudinal wave the disturbance is parallel to the direction of travel (compressions and stretches along a spring or in sound).

items.title: Get It? (amplitude, frequency, wavelength vs. speed)

answer.html: Changing amplitude, frequency, or wavelength does not change the speed of a mechanical wave (except water surface waves). Speed depends on the medium and wave type. Changing frequency just changes wavelength to keep 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 the same.

items.title: Figure 10 caption: Determine the period of the wave in the displacement-versus-time graph.

body.html: In the right-hand graph, successive crests are at 𝑡≈0.1 s and 𝑡≈0.5 s (zero crossings at 0.0, 0.2, 0.4 s going up/down).
𝑇= 0.5 s −0.1 s = 0.4 s (also 𝑓= 1 / 𝑇= 2.5 Hz). The left graph gives 𝜆≈0.4 m (crests at about 0, 0.4, 0.8 m).

check.html: The wave speed would be 𝜆/ 𝑇≈0.4 / 0.4 = 1 m/s, a reasonable rope-wave speed.

items.title: 14: Clock chime heard 515 m away 1.50 s later; 𝑓= 436 Hz.

body.html: 𝛥𝑑= 515 m, 𝛥𝑡= 1.50 s, 𝑓= 436 Hz. Find (a) 𝑣, (b) 𝑇, (c) 𝜆 .
𝑣= 𝛥𝑑/ 𝛥𝑡, 𝑇= 1 / 𝑓, 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓.

answer.html: 𝑇= 2.29 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> s

check.html: 343 m/s is the speed of sound in air near 20 °C.

items.title: 15: How are 𝜆, 𝑓, and 𝑣 related, and how do they depend on the medium and wave type?

answer.html: 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆 (so 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓). The speed depends only on the medium and the type of wave (and temperature), not on frequency or amplitude. The frequency depends only on the source. So when the medium changes, 𝑣 and 𝜆 change while 𝑓 stays the same.

items.title: 16: Speed of a wave with 𝑓= 3.50 Hz and 𝜆= 0.700 m. 𝑣= 𝑓𝜆= (3.50 Hz)(0.700 m) = 2.45 m/s
17: Effect on frequency of increasing the wavelength by 50 percent (wave on a rope).

body.html: The speed is set by the rope, so it stays constant; 𝑓= 𝑣/ 𝜆.

answer.html: The frequency decreases to two-thirds of the original (about a 33% decrease).

items.title: 18: 𝑣= 15.0 m/s in a string, 𝑓= 6.00 Hz. Wavelength?
19: Five wavelengths every 0.100 s; 𝜆= 1.20 cm. Speed?

body.html: Frequency 𝑓= 5 / 0.100 s = 50.0 Hz. Then:

check.html: Equivalent: five wavelengths = 6.00 cm in 0.100 s = 0.600 m/s.

items.title: 20: 𝑓= 20.0 Hz, compressions 0.600 m apart. Speed?

body.html: The distance between successive compressions is one wavelength.

items.title: 21: Frequency change when the period doubles.

answer.html: The frequency is halved.

items.title: 22: Change in wavelength when the period is reduced by one-half.

body.html: 𝜆= 𝑣𝑇 and 𝑣 is fixed by the medium.

answer.html: The wavelength is cut in half.

items.title: 23: Speed increases to 1.5 times with constant frequency. Wavelength?

answer.html: The wavelength increases by a factor of 1.5 (50% longer).

items.title: 24 (Challenge): Hiker's echo (Figure 11).

body.html: Figure 11 shows the cliff 465 m away. The echo returns after 𝛥𝑡= 2.75 s. The sound travels there and back, so the distance is 2(465 m) = 930 m. 𝜆= 0.750 m. Find 𝑣, 𝑓, 𝑇.

answer.html: 𝑓= 451 Hz
𝑇= 2.22 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> s

check.html: 338 m/s is close to the speed of sound (a cool day).

items.title: 25: Demonstrate that a transverse wave transports energy but not matter.

answer.html: Tie a ribbon (or a piece of tape) to the middle of a long rope or spring toy held by your partner and send a pulse along it. The ribbon moves up and down and returns to its starting position (no matter moved along the rope), while the pulse travels the full length. Energy transport: the pulse can knock over a light object (a stack of paper cups) at the far end, or your partner feels the jerk on their hand.

items.title: 26: Shaking the rope faster with the same hand motion.

body.html: Amplitude is set by the hand's distance. Frequency is set by the hand (source). The speed is set by the rope. 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓.

answer.html: Amplitude: unchanged. Frequency: increases. Period: decreases. Velocity: unchanged (rope's property). Wavelength: decreases (shorter waves, since 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓).

items.title: 27: Describe longitudinal waves. What media transmit them?

answer.html: In a longitudinal wave the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, producing alternating compressions and rarefactions (stretched regions), as in sound or a pushed coiled spring toy. They travel through solids, liquids, and gases, since all of them resist compression.

items.title: 28: Pulse speeds in a coiled spring toy, a rope, and a metal rod.

answer.html: No pulse arrives instantly in any of them. In the coiled spring toy the pulse is slow enough to watch, and it takes noticeable time to reach the far end. In a rope it moves faster (stiffer, more tension). In a metal rod it is fastest, thousands of m/s, and the far end seems to move right away. Speed depends on the medium's stiffness and density, and the metal rod is much stiffer.

items.title: 29 (Critical Thinking): Why doesn't heavy rain make large waves?

answer.html: Each raindrop carries little energy, so each makes a tiny wave. Drops land at random places and times, so their waves are out of phase and partly cancel (destructive interference) instead of adding up. A swimmer delivers much more energy in one coordinated disturbance, so the wave amplitude is large. Waves need coordinated (in-phase) driving to build amplitude.
